## When ordinary linear regression cannot model the response

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-generalized-linear-models/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: b899000159010f73fc44c76394c3a85d6375595b9c636e6da4cfa5dce09ec12d; role: concept -->

It is not an independent participant-level summary.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Ordinary linear regression lets a conditional mean range over the real line and treats residual variance as constant. A binary linguistic response violates both commitments. We can see the problem in the **SuperTelicity cloze data** of White, Cao, Grimm, and Glass's working manuscript, *The preservation of telicity under sense locality* (n.d.). The credential-gated source repository is pinned at commit `e45277ce466719c1a03629f6ccf1e12db9904421`; the immutable CC BY-SA teaching table makes the analyzed data public with sentence text removed. Each row records one participant's choice of *in* or *for* after an event description. It is not an independent participant-level summary.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd
:::

## The support problem in observed data {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-generalized-linear-models/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: b899000159010f73fc44c76394c3a85d6375595b9c636e6da4cfa5dce09ec12d; role: math -->

For $Y_i=1$ when participant $i$ chooses *in* and $Y_i=0$ otherwise,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1\mid\mathbf x_i)=\pi_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $Y_i=1$ when participant $i$ chooses *in* and $Y_i=0$ otherwise,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1\mid\mathbf x_i)=\pi_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd
:::

## The support problem in observed data

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-generalized-linear-models/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: b899000159010f73fc44c76394c3a85d6375595b9c636e6da4cfa5dce09ec12d; role: concept -->

A logit model instead sets $\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A linear probability model, $\pi_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$, does not constrain $\pi_i$ to $[0,1]$. A logit model instead sets $\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd
:::

## The support problem in observed data

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-generalized-linear-models/09-concept; notes-page: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: b899000159010f73fc44c76394c3a85d6375595b9c636e6da4cfa5dce09ec12d; role: concept -->

These population fits expose that architecture; they do not reproduce the manuscript's Bayesian mixed model or account for repeated participants and sentences.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This is also a variance problem: Bernoulli variance is determined by the mean, rather than by one constant residual variance. A generalized linear model repairs both pieces by choosing a response family with the right support and a link that constrains the mean. These population fits expose that architecture; they do not reproduce the manuscript's Bayesian mixed model or account for repeated participants and sentences.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.qmd

## Link functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/link-functions/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/link-functions.qmd; note-sha256: de31e2e101de42af6e06e8ca699653f57ce0da3c568661a265f1d0fbacb85479; role: concept -->

A **link function** maps a constrained conditional mean to the real-valued linear predictor.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **link function** maps a constrained conditional mean to the real-valued linear predictor. We continue with SuperTelicity, where the response is an *in* choice and the first-use source and design are introduced on the preceding page.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/link-functions.qmd

## Link functions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/link-functions/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/link-functions.qmd; note-sha256: de31e2e101de42af6e06e8ca699653f57ce0da3c568661a265f1d0fbacb85479; role: math -->

For a Bernoulli mean $0<\pi_i<1$, the logit link and its inverse are

$$
g(\pi_i)=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
g^{-1}(\eta_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}=\pi_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a Bernoulli mean $0<\pi_i<1$, the logit link and its inverse are

$$
g(\pi_i)=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
g^{-1}(\eta_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta_i}}=\pi_i.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/link-functions.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/link-functions/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/link-functions.qmd; note-sha256: de31e2e101de42af6e06e8ca699653f57ce0da3c568661a265f1d0fbacb85479; role: concept -->

The fitted SuperTelicity model supplies actual values on both scales.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## The inverse link keeps predictions valid

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/link-functions/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/link-functions.qmd; note-sha256: de31e2e101de42af6e06e8ca699653f57ce0da3c568661a265f1d0fbacb85479; role: concept -->

It connects the linear predictor to the family mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The model is additive in $\eta_i$ but curved in $\pi_i$. A constant coefficient is a constant change in log odds, not in probability. The link changes neither the Bernoulli support nor the observed response. It connects the linear predictor to the family mean.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/link-functions.qmd
:::

## The inverse link keeps predictions valid

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/link-functions/08-concept; notes-page: regression-models/link-functions.qmd; note-sha256: de31e2e101de42af6e06e8ca699653f57ce0da3c568661a265f1d0fbacb85479; role: concept -->

It is not a device for making a histogram look normal.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For count means the analogous construction uses $\log\lambda_i=\eta_i$ and $\lambda_i=e^{\eta_i}>0$. Thus the choice of link follows the support of the conditional mean. It is not a device for making a histogram look normal.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/link-functions.qmd
:::

## Generalized linear models

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/generalized-linear-models/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: c65bd518957c0fed70f8783cc56f776d9806201a0fbfe8eab7e9155a468d22d7; role: concept -->

The SuperTelicity *in* versus *for* response makes each part observable.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **generalized linear model (GLM)** has three distinct parts: (i) a response distribution, (ii) a linear predictor, and (iii) a link between the distribution's conditional mean and that predictor. The SuperTelicity *in* versus *for* response makes each part observable.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd
:::

## Generalized linear models {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/generalized-linear-models/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd; note-sha256: c65bd518957c0fed70f8783cc56f776d9806201a0fbfe8eab7e9155a468d22d7; role: math -->

The response component is $Y_i\mid\pi_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)$, the systematic component is

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i,
$$

and the link gives

$$
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
\pi_i=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i)]}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The response component is $Y_i\mid\pi_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)$, the systematic component is

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i,
$$

and the link gives

$$
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
\pi_i=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i)]}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd
:::

## The exponential family {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: math -->

Many GLM response distributions share the **exponential-family form**. For a discrete member, write the PMF as

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Many GLM response distributions share the **exponential-family form**. For a discrete member, write the PMF as

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd
:::

## The exponential family

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: concept -->

We use (p) only for the discrete Bernoulli member below.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an absolutely continuous member, the same form is written as a PDF (f(y\mid\theta,\phi)). We use (p) only for the discrete Bernoulli member below.

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: concept -->

To make those roles concrete, we derive the Bernoulli member from the observed SuperTelicity choices.

## The exponential family {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: math -->

For $y_i\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $y_i\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.
$$

## The exponential family {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: math -->

Set $\theta_i=\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)]$. Because $\pi_i=e^{\theta_i}/(1+e^{\theta_i})$,

$$
\log p(y_i\mid\theta_i)=y_i\theta_i-\log(1+e^{\theta_i}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Set $\theta_i=\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)]$. Because $\pi_i=e^{\theta_i}/(1+e^{\theta_i})$,

$$
\log p(y_i\mid\theta_i)=y_i\theta_i-\log(1+e^{\theta_i}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd
:::

## The exponential family

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: concept -->

Differentiating $b$ recovers $b'(\theta)=\pi$ and $b''(\theta)=\pi(1-\pi)$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus $b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta)$ and $a(\phi)=1$. Differentiating $b$ recovers $b'(\theta)=\pi$ and $b''(\theta)=\pi(1-\pi)$.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd
:::

## The exponential family

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exponential-family/08-concept; notes-page: regression-models/exponential-family.qmd; note-sha256: 0655d99a2d6ea90ddc51e7a02cb42bb9e2cf50b9396bee6fbaa02d28b7254165; role: concept -->

The exponential-family notation organizes those distinctions; it does not remove them.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The shared form links distributions to GLM computation, but it does not make the families interchangeable. Bernoulli, Poisson, and normal models retain different supports and mean-variance relations. The exponential-family notation organizes those distinctions; it does not remove them.

[Sources]

## Sufficient statistics

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/sufficient-statistics/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/sufficient-statistics.qmd; note-sha256: dda6f31ba9bdfa8c79a4fdac6e5573701a7e350c104435a608f51c1e5dc4d9ae; role: concept -->

For an intercept-only Bernoulli model of the SuperTelicity choices, the sufficient information is the row count and number of *in* responses.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A statistic is **sufficient** for a parameter when, under the stated model, it retains all sample information about that parameter. For an intercept-only Bernoulli model of the SuperTelicity choices, the sufficient information is the row count and number of *in* responses.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sufficient-statistics.qmd
:::

## Sufficient statistics {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/sufficient-statistics/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/sufficient-statistics.qmd; note-sha256: dda6f31ba9bdfa8c79a4fdac6e5573701a7e350c104435a608f51c1e5dc4d9ae; role: math -->

The joint likelihood is

$$
L(\pi;\mathbf y)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i}
=\pi^{\sum_i y_i}(1-\pi)^{n-\sum_i y_i}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The joint likelihood is

$$
L(\pi;\mathbf y)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\pi^{y_i}(1-\pi)^{1-y_i}
=\pi^{\sum_i y_i}(1-\pi)^{n-\sum_i y_i}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sufficient-statistics.qmd

## Iteratively reweighted least squares

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd; note-sha256: c6fa42870a9c4e328bda2a83d6179f04646bc2ab8d67cfe53c51976e103baafa; role: concept -->

We can follow that sequence for the SuperTelicity verb-type model.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Logistic regression has no ordinary least-squares solution because the inverse logit makes the likelihood nonlinear in the coefficients. **Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)** solves a sequence of local weighted least-squares problems. We can follow that sequence for the SuperTelicity verb-type model.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd
:::

## Iteratively reweighted least squares {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd; note-sha256: c6fa42870a9c4e328bda2a83d6179f04646bc2ab8d67cfe53c51976e103baafa; role: math -->

At iteration $t$, let

$$
\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)},\quad
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}),
$$

$$
w_i^{(t)}=\mu_i^{(t)}[1-\mu_i^{(t)}],\quad
z_i^{(t)}=\eta_i^{(t)}+\frac{y_i-\mu_i^{(t)}}{w_i^{(t)}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At iteration $t$, let

$$
\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)},\quad
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}),
$$

$$
w_i^{(t)}=\mu_i^{(t)}[1-\mu_i^{(t)}],\quad
z_i^{(t)}=\eta_i^{(t)}+\frac{y_i-\mu_i^{(t)}}{w_i^{(t)}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd
:::

## Iteratively reweighted least squares {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd; note-sha256: c6fa42870a9c4e328bda2a83d6179f04646bc2ab8d67cfe53c51976e103baafa; role: math -->

The update is

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf z^{(t)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The update is

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf z^{(t)}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd
:::

## Iteratively reweighted least squares

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd; note-sha256: c6fa42870a9c4e328bda2a83d6179f04646bc2ab8d67cfe53c51976e103baafa; role: concept -->

IRLS is local least squares, not a claim that the Bernoulli data have become Gaussian.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The plotted path records successive local weighted-least-squares solutions. The working response $\mathbf z$ is algorithmic, whereas the observed response remains the original vector of *in* and *for* choices; the final coefficients agree with `glm()` to the asserted tolerance. Thus IRLS is local least squares, not a claim that the Bernoulli data have become Gaussian.

## Deviance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/deviance/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/deviance.qmd; note-sha256: 2172c0d3be943fa2271dc62614f81981870da50099f61e46dac2a6ae5e1a163b; role: math -->

If $\ell(\widehat\theta)$ is the fitted log likelihood and $\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is the saturated log likelihood,

$$
D=2\{\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\widehat\theta)\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Deviance** measures how far a fitted likelihood is from the saturated model, which assigns one fitted mean to each observation. If $\ell(\widehat\theta)$ is the fitted log likelihood and $\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is the saturated log likelihood,

$$
D=2\{\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\widehat\theta)\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/deviance.qmd
:::

## Deviance

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/deviance/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/deviance.qmd; note-sha256: 2172c0d3be943fa2271dc62614f81981870da50099f61e46dac2a6ae5e1a163b; role: concept -->

We compare four population models for the same SuperTelicity rows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For Bernoulli rows, the saturated contribution is zero, so residual deviance is $-2\ell(\widehat\theta)$. We compare four population models for the same SuperTelicity rows.

## Odds and log odds {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/odds-and-log-odds/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/odds-and-log-odds.qmd; note-sha256: d54bdf33ff05c4518b25a18993e2597b0ffc45224924d641024464219f98d4e4; role: math -->

For a probability $p$, the **odds** and **log odds** are

$$
\operatorname{odds}(p)=\frac{p}{1-p},
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\frac{p}{1-p}.
$$

::: {.notes}

$$

$$

## Deviance residuals {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/deviance-residuals/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/deviance-residuals.qmd; note-sha256: 6bce5f3d971e330a02b2d518949294f97de28fb015ee0d8b4ffe921f60aeabe7; role: math -->

A deviance residual assigns each observation a signed share of model deviance. For Bernoulli logistic regression,

$$
r_i^{D}=\operatorname{sign}(y_i-\widehat\pi_i)
\sqrt{2\left[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\widehat\pi_i}+
(1-y_i)\log\frac{1-y_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}\right]},
$$

with zero-times-log-zero terms defined as zero.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A deviance residual assigns each observation a signed share of model deviance. For Bernoulli logistic regression,

$$

\sqrt{2\left[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\widehat\pi_i}+
(1-y_i)\log\frac{1-y_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i}\right]},
$$

with zero-times-log-zero terms defined as zero.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/deviance-residuals.qmd
:::

## Ordinal regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordinal-regression/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fb9288a6ff5fa012c9b410ea18d428d2521253a6c08785551294972946fc2ae0; role: concept -->

The direct and conditional tasks recruited separate samples; the task prefix on `respondent_id` prevents 29 reused numeric labels from becoming false repeated measurements.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An ordinal response has ordered categories but no defensible numerical spacing. We use **MegaVeridicality v1**, the *no*-*maybe*-*yes* veridicality judgments described by White and Rawlins (2018 paper; CC BY-SA project release). Each row is one judgment for a verb, polarity, task, item, and task-specific respondent. The direct and conditional tasks recruited separate samples; the task prefix on `respondent_id` prevents 29 reused numeric labels from becoming false repeated measurements.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Cumulative logits {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordinal-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fb9288a6ff5fa012c9b410ea18d428d2521253a6c08785551294972946fc2ae0; role: math -->

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_1<\kappa_2$ and linear predictor $\eta_i$,

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\leq c)=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

With the logistic CDF $F$, the category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_1<\kappa_2$ and linear predictor $\eta_i$,

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\leq c)=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

With the logistic CDF $F$, the category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

## Interpreting one coefficient at both boundaries

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordinal-regression/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fb9288a6ff5fa012c9b410ea18d428d2521253a6c08785551294972946fc2ae0; role: concept -->

It does not imply an equal change in each category probability, which is why the complete fitted distribution remains the primary interpretation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A positive coefficient increases the linear predictor and shifts probability toward higher responses. Under proportional odds, the same coefficient applies to *maybe* or *yes* versus *no* and to *yes* versus *no* or *maybe*. It does not imply an equal change in each category probability, which is why the complete fitted distribution remains the primary interpretation.

[Sources]

https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf
https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/
:::

The negative-polarity and polarity-by-task coefficients differ across boundaries, so one shared location shift is a useful baseline but an imperfect description. ## Poisson regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/poisson-regression/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-regression.qmd; note-sha256: cd86cca275e4116e5dcf4bd1de8d6bc336842c24eecdac1db14c6a43d3b771cf; role: concept -->

That repository states no data license, so these notes do not redistribute it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Poisson regression models a nonnegative count with a positive conditional mean. We use Nettle's (1998) country-level study of language diversity and climate. One row is one country; the response is its reported language count, mean growing season (MGS) is the ecological predictor, and area measures geographic opportunity. The teaching table comes from Bodo Winter's course-data repository. That repository states no data license, so these notes do not redistribute it.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1006/jaar.1998.0328
https://github.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data/blob/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/
:::

## Poisson regression {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/poisson-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-regression.qmd; note-sha256: cd86cca275e4116e5dcf4bd1de8d6bc336842c24eecdac1db14c6a43d3b771cf; role: math -->

The model is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\lambda_i,
$$

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The model is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\lambda_i,
$$

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1006/jaar.1998.0328
https://github.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data/blob/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/
:::

$\lambda_i/A_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i)$ is the fitted language rate per square kilometer.

## Poisson regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/poisson-regression/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/poisson-regression.qmd; note-sha256: cd86cca275e4116e5dcf4bd1de8d6bc336842c24eecdac1db14c6a43d3b771cf; role: concept -->

Fixing it to one narrows the question and does not reproduce the paper or support a causal ecological claim.

A one-month increase in MGS multiplies the fitted rate by 1.284, conditional on the teaching specification. Nettle instead estimated the log-area coefficient. Fixing it to one narrows the question and does not reproduce the paper or support a causal ecological claim.

## Exposure offsets

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exposure-offsets/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/exposure-offsets.qmd; note-sha256: c454395cdd03f284d1c0164fa135f555d8fcbfd93f4d45372889fdafd1d23875; role: concept -->

An **offset** fixes the exposure coefficient rather than estimating it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A count is inseparable from its opportunity window. For Nettle's country data, area is a proposed exposure: larger countries provide more geographic space in which languages are counted. An **offset** fixes the exposure coefficient rather than estimating it.

[Sources]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/
:::

## Exposure offsets {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/exposure-offsets/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/exposure-offsets.qmd; note-sha256: c454395cdd03f284d1c0164fa135f555d8fcbfd93f4d45372889fdafd1d23875; role: math -->

If $A_i$ is area and $r_i$ is the expected language rate per unit area, then

$$
\lambda_i=A_i r_i,
$$

so

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\log r_i
=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $A_i$ is area and $r_i$ is the expected language rate per unit area, then

$$
\lambda_i=A_i r_i,
$$

so

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\log r_i
=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/

## Count overdispersion

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/count-overdispersion/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/count-overdispersion.qmd; note-sha256: 35c21f52f582f9fcc949bef8a465e7b4090c939a25b104ff6c90071b865193ac; role: concept -->

We diagnose it in the Nettle teaching model with Pearson residuals.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Poisson regression requires conditional mean and variance to be equal. **Overdispersion** occurs when the remaining variation is larger than that requirement permits. We diagnose it in the Nettle teaching model with Pearson residuals.

[Sources]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/

$$
\widehat\phi=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_i
\frac{(y_i-\widehat\lambda_i)^2}{\widehat\lambda_i}.

[Transcript]

More observed zeros than a Poisson model predicts do not by themselves establish a separate zero-generating process. so ordinary heterogeneity can increase both tails, including zero mass.

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-not-beta-sliders/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/why-not-beta-sliders.qmd; note-sha256: e2f8300d8ee1c9daba1656692ad850180247470012eb28fda9d5b9e9a4eee266; role: concept -->

MegaNegRaising contains exact zeros and ones on both recorded sliders, so ordinary beta regression assigns those observations zero probability.

## Why ordinary beta regression does not fit endpoint sliders {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-not-beta-sliders/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/why-not-beta-sliders.qmd; note-sha256: e2f8300d8ee1c9daba1656692ad850180247470012eb28fda9d5b9e9a4eee266; role: math -->

For $0<y<1$, a mean-precision beta parameterization is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\mu_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $0<y<1$, a mean-precision beta parameterization is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\mu_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/why-not-beta-sliders.qmd
:::

## Why ordinary beta regression does not fit endpoint sliders {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/why-not-beta-sliders/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/why-not-beta-sliders.qmd; note-sha256: e2f8300d8ee1c9daba1656692ad850180247470012eb28fda9d5b9e9a4eee266; role: math -->

Neither density value at an endpoint is a probability mass. A common workaround nudges every observation with

$$
y_i^*=\frac{y_i(n-1)+1/2}{n}.
$$

::: {.notes}

## Ordered-beta regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordered-beta-regression/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 1c40d61cfb4ae4399d71374d80a3b85d16b970584c963ebf593ae9e26efbfcc3; role: concept -->

We fit the same population formula to both MegaNegRaising sliders, as prespecified in the dataset audit.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Ordered-beta regression** represents three observable regions: $Y_i=0$, $0<Y_i<1$, and $Y_i=1$. We fit the same population formula to both MegaNegRaising sliders, as prespecified in the dataset audit.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.qmd
:::

## Ordered-beta regression {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordered-beta-regression/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 1c40d61cfb4ae4399d71374d80a3b85d16b970584c963ebf593ae9e26efbfcc3; role: math -->

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_0<\kappa_1$ and $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=0)=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(0<Y_i<1)=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)=1-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_0<\kappa_1$ and $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=0)=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(0<Y_i<1)=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)=1-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.qmd
:::

## Ordered-beta regression {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: generalized-linear-models/ordered-beta-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 1c40d61cfb4ae4399d71374d80a3b85d16b970584c963ebf593ae9e26efbfcc3; role: math -->

Conditional on the interior,

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
\qquad \mu_i=F(\eta_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Conditional on the interior,

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
\qquad \mu_i=F(\eta_i).
$$
